text: Ordering from the Service Catalog creates two different records, not one. Understanding that split — and why it exists — is the real implementation foundation this chapter builds on.

The sc_request table holds the overall order: one record per checkout, no matter how many items were in the cart. The sc_req_item table holds the individual line items — one record per catalog item ordered. Order a laptop, a monitor, and a software license in one checkout, and you get one sc_request and three sc_req_item records, each pointing back at that same request.

That split exists because fulfillment happens item by item, often by entirely different teams. IT hardware fulfills the laptop and monitor; a licensing team fulfills the software. Each Requested Item carries its own state and its own assignment group, moving through fulfillment independently, while the Request stays the one place the requester checks for their whole order.

Because items can be in different states at once, the Request needs its own rollup status, calculated from the items underneath it rather than set by hand. If two items are Closed Complete and one is still Work in Progress, the Request should read something like Partially Complete — not Closed Complete just because most of the order is done. Close the Request early, and you tell the requester their order is finished while a license is still sitting in someone's queue.

This is also why an SLA almost always belongs on the Requested Item, not the overall Request. A software license might need to be fulfilled within two business days; hardware in the same order might reasonably take five. One SLA clock on the Request would fit neither item correctly the moment a checkout mixes two different kinds of fulfillment work.

One reference field — request, on sc_req_item — is what makes every rollup and every related list work. Next, we look at the fulfillment workflows that actually move a Requested Item through its states, from Open to Closed Complete.
